title: Constantinople (381)
hookLine: the council completes the creed: the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life
carry: the lord, the giver of life

lines: NICAEA: AND IN THE HOLY SPIRIT. FULL STOP.
THE SAME QUESTION, ABOUT THE SPIRIT.
cards: The creed from Nicaea spent a long time on the Son. Begotten, not made. Of one substance with the Father.
Then it reached the Holy Spirit and said, in effect, just this: and in the Holy Spirit. Full stop. For a while that seemed enough.
Then people began asking the same kind of question about the Spirit that Arius had asked about the Son. Is the Spirit God, or a power God sends, or something God made?

So bishops gathered again, in Constantinople, the city that carried Constantine's name, where Gregory had preached in his small chapel and then stepped down. What they added is still said in churches.

teach.h: THE LORD: A TITLE THAT BELONGS TO GOD.
teach.b: Here's the fuller creed that came out of Constantinople, in the old English of the Book of Common Prayer. On the Spirit, it now says: "And I believe in the Holy Ghost, The Lord and giver of life." Two titles.
First, Lord: the same word the creed uses for Jesus, a title that belongs to God. Second, giver of life. In the Greek that's one word, zoopoion, the life-maker.

teach.h: THE GIVER OF LIFE: BREATH IN THE DUST.
teach.b: Some readers hear in it Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust and "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."
And Jesus in John's Gospel: "It is the spirit that quickeneth." Quickeneth: makes alive.

teach.h: AND THE SON: WHERE CHURCHES DIFFER.
teach.b: The next line is where churches today differ. The council's Greek says the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Later, in the West, the words and the Son were added, and the Prayer Book text has them.

Orthodox Christians say the creed without those words. In the West, Catholic Christians, and Protestant churches that use the creed, generally say it with them. That phrase has been argued over for a long time.
Then the creed adds: "Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, Who spake by the Prophets." Worshipped together: not a lesser helper, but one God, Father, Son and Spirit.

This is the creed later called, simply, the Nicene Creed. So the creed said in churches on Sunday carries both councils, and its closing section, on the Spirit, runs on to the church, baptism and the life to come.

how: Christians in Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed together in worship, Orthodox churches without the words and the Son, most Western churches with them.

games.q: you're a bishop at Constantinople. people ask whether the Spirit is God or a power God sends. what do you add to the creed?

practice: Let your breathing slow, and notice the breath coming in without forcing it.

Genesis pictures life starting with a breath, so let each breath in be the words giver of, and each breath out, life; if you pray, you can say the creed's line silently instead: the Lord, and giver of life.
If you don't, simply notice the breath arriving on its own.

orig.note: Greek: the life-giving one, the giver of life. the creed's word for the Holy Spirit.
